title: Ram Manohar Lohia

cards.b:
Ram Manohar Lohia (1910-67) was a socialist leader who tried to make socialism Indian. He stressed caste, language and rural India, and is the intellectual root of much OBC politics in the Hindi belt.

He appears in Paper I's Indian thought and in questions on non-Congressism and backward-caste politics.

Lohia felt that Marx's class analysis, built on Europe, is incomplete for India, where caste and class overlap. His slogan: caste is 'closed class' and class is 'open caste'. Without breaking caste, there can be no equality.

He also rejected both the Western capitalist and the Soviet models as 'twin evils' using huge machines and centralised power.

He called for simultaneous struggles against seven injustices.

  1. Inequality of man and woman
  2. Inequality of colour
  3. Caste (inequality by birth)
  4. Foreign domination, and for national and world freedom
  5. Economic inequality
  6. Violation of private life by the state
  7. Armaments, in favour of satyagraha

Lohia proposed a four-pillar state (Chaukhamba Raj): village, district, province and Centre, each with real power. Power should be shared down to the village.

He favoured small-unit technology (like the charkha in modern form), not giant machines, in a Gandhian way. He attacked the 'permanent government' of the elite.

The Samyukta Socialist Party slogan is credited to him: 'Sansopa ne bandhi gaanth, pichhde pawen sau mein saath', meaning backward castes, women and the poor should get 60 per cent of opportunities. He backed reservation in jobs and politics beyond SC/ST.

He also campaigned for Indian languages with the slogan Angrezi Hatao (remove English as the language of power).

cards.h: Wheel of History and Guilt of Partition
cards.b:
Wheel of History (1955) argues that history moves between periods of caste-based hierarchy and class-based change. Marx, Gandhi and Socialism (1963) mixes the three. In Guilt of Divided India (1960) he blames Congress leaders' weariness and the British for Partition.

Keep the name, the year and the one-line claim ready. These three details are what examiners look for when they check a concept.
Lohia's non-Congressism (from 1963) urged opposition parties to unite against Congress dominance. It worked in 1967, though most of the SVD governments were short lived.

• Aggressive anti-English stand hurt the south and modern education.
  • The Samyukta Socialist Party was fragmented, with little organisation.
  • Later 'Lohiaites' (Mulayam Singh Yadav, Lalu Prasad, Nitish Kumar) are accused of dynastic and caste politics, far from his vision.
  • Supporters: he put caste, gender and decentralisation on the agenda before others.

Mandal reservations (1990), Panchayati Raj and the OBC political rise in the Hindi belt draw on his thought. On gender he raised violence and equality, and on caste he influenced 1967 coalition politics.
